extracted.intended_audience: amateur and professional astronomers, observatory designers, and practical observers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for making accurate telescopic and meridian observations, designing and siting observatories and instruments, and for astronomical timekeeping (transit instruments, clocks, mural circles, sextants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for 'good' observing hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Not more than one hundred good hours in a year could be obtained for observation with Herschel's great telescope. By 'good' hours, Herschel means that the sky must be very clear, the moon absent, no twilight, no haziness, no violent wind, and no sudden change of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only times when sky transparency and stability meet all listed conditions; these factors are magnified by telescopes. Warm climates tend to provide more such hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climatic preference for observing sites
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general fact, the warmer climates enjoy a much finer sky for the astronomer than the colder, having many more clear evenings, a short twilight, and less change of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sites with fewer temperature changes, short twilight, and lower hygrometric turbidity (watery vapor more perfectly dissolved in hot air), as these yield clearer skies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer preparation and dark adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain preparation of the observer himself is also requisite for the nicest observations with the telescope. He must be free from all agitation, and the eye must not recently have been exposed to a strong light, which contracts the pupil of the eye. Indeed, for delicate observations, the observer should remain for some time beforehand in a dark room, to let the pupil of the eye dilate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid activities that cause breathlessness or recent exposure to bright light (e.g., ascending observatory stairs after being in a strongly-lighted room). Allow time in darkness before delicate observing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit people near the instrument during refined observations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the more refined observations, only one or two persons ought to be near the instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize nearby activity to reduce disturbances and distraction when making precise observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadiness of instrument and observatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Want of steadiness is a great difficulty attending the use of the highest magnifiers; for the motions of the instrument are magnified as well as the object. Hence, in the structure of observatories, the greatest pains is requisite, to avoid all tremor, and to give to the instruments all possible steadiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observatory foundations and instrument mounts to eliminate tremor (deep masonry, isolation from floors/walls) and avoid site disturbances (public roads, passing carriages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer low powers for general viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, low powers afford better views of the heavenly bodies than very high magnifiers. A good light and large field are qualities, for most purposes, more important than great magnifying power; and it must be borne in mind, that, as we increase the magnifying power in a given instrument, we diminish both the illumination and the field of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower magnification to maximize illumination and field unless the target specifically requires high power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match magnifying power to the object observed
rubrics_metrics.description: Different objects require different magnifying powers; and a telescope is usually furnished with several varieties of powers, one of which is best fitted for viewing the moon, another for Jupiter, and a still higher power for Saturn. Comets require only the lowest magnifiers ... for certain double stars ... we require very high magnifiers, in order to separate these minute objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select eyepiece/power according to target: low power for comets (max light and field), moderate for planets, high power for resolving close double stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare novices with drawings and explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we exhibit celestial objects to inexperienced observers, it is useful to precede the view with good drawings of the objects, accompanied by an explanation of what each appearance, exhibited in the telescope, indicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show annotated drawings and describe expected telescope views before letting novices look; this orients their expectations and aids recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observatory site selection: unobstructed view and atmospheric cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The great objects to be attained in the construction of an observatory are, a commanding and unobstructed view of the heavens; freedom from causes that affect the transparency and uniform state of the atmosphere, such as fires, smoke, or marshy grounds; mechanical facilities for the management of instruments, and, especially, every precaution that is necessary to secure perfect steadiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose elevated, open sites away from urban smoke, marshes, and other local sources of atmospheric disturbance; ensure mechanical access and working space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observatory mechanical isolation and foundation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures of solid masonry are commenced deep enough in the ground to be unaffected by frost, and built up to the height required, without any connexion with the other parts of the building. ... The stone pillar is carried up separate from the walls and floors of the building, so as to be entirely free from the agitations to which they are liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mount heavy instruments on isolated masonry piers or pillars founded below frost depth and decoupled from building floors/walls to prevent transmitted vibrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movable dome design for instrument access
rubrics_metrics.description: Many observatories are furnished with a movable dome for a roof, capable of revolving on rollers, so that instruments penetrating through the roof may be easily brought to bear upon any point at or near the zenith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a rotating dome or equivalent to allow unobstructed pointing of instruments across the sky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of transit instrument and astronomical clock for meridian work
rubrics_metrics.description: A very large proportion of all astronomical observations are taken on the meridian, by means of the transit instrument and clock. ... When a body, in its diurnal revolution, comes to the meridian, it is at its highest point above the horizon, and is then least affected by refraction and parallax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip observatories with a well-mounted transit instrument and an accurately regulated clock for high-precision meridian observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transit instrument setup and leveling
rubrics_metrics.description: The transit instrument is a telescope which is fixed permanently in the meridian, and moves only in that plane. ... Near the circle may be seen a spirit-level, which serves to show when the axis is exactly on a level with the horizon. The framework is made of solid metal ... It stands on screws, which not only afford a steady support, but are useful for adjusting the instrument to a perfect level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the transit axis is exactly level (use spirit-level and fine screw adjustments) and mount on a solid, vibration-free support (stone pillar if possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of transit instrument and clock to measure right ascension
rubrics_metrics.description: When a star is on the meridian, the clock itself shows its right ascension ... If we note the interval of time between the passage of any two stars, as shown by the clock, we have a measure of the number of degrees by which they are distant from each other in right ascension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record meridian passage times with a sidereal-regulated clock; time differences yield differences in right ascension directly (15 degrees per hour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for determining declination via pole distance
rubrics_metrics.description: By declination ... When a star is passing the meridian, if, on the instant of crossing the meridian wire of the telescope, we take its distance from the north pole ... and subtract this distance from ninety degrees, the remainder will be the distance from the equator, which is the declination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure star's meridian distance from the pole (where pole position is known/equal to latitude) and compute declination as 90° minus pole-distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noon-mark construction for local noon without telescope
rubrics_metrics.description: A noon-mark may easily be made by the aid of the transit instrument. ... Upon a smooth, level plane, freely exposed to the sun, with a pair of compasses describe a circle. In the centre ... erect a perpendicular wire ... mark the shadow where it falls on the circle in morning and afternoon; take midpoint between those two points and draw a line to the centre, and it will be a true meridian line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct noon-marks on a level plane by noting symmetric shadow points and bisecting them to establish the meridian; best performed around mid-June for sharper definition and agreement with clocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve noon-mark precision with an aperture
rubrics_metrics.description: If the upper end of the wire is flattened, and a small hole is made in it, through which the sun may shine, the instant when this bright spot falls upon the circle will be better defined than the termination of the shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small aperture at the wire tip to project a bright spot for more precise timing of crossing points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mural circle purpose and size for minute-angle measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The mural circle is a graduated circle, usually of very large size, fixed permanently in the plane of the meridian ... It is made of large size, sometimes twenty feet in diameter, in order that very small angles may be measured on its limb; for it is obvious that a small angle, as one second, will be a larger space on the limb of an instrument, in proportion as the instrument itself is larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use very large-diameter mural circles (and attach them to stable walls) when minute angular measurement (seconds of arc) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readings via microscope and micrometer for fine subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: On the rim of the instrument ... you may observe a microscope. This is attached to a micrometer,--a delicate piece of apparatus, used for reading the minute subdivisions of angles; ... each of these spaces may again be subdivided into seconds by the micrometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ microscopes and micrometers to magnify and subdivide limb graduations to reach seconds-level angular measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach large instruments to massive structure for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very difficult to keep so large an instrument perfectly steady; and therefore it is attached to a massive wall of solid masonry, and is hence called a mural circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix large, sensitive instruments to massive, stable masonry walls or piers to minimize warping and motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of precision instrument-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of constructing astronomical instruments is one which requires such refined mechanical genius,--so superior a mind to devise, and so delicate a hand to execute,--that the most celebrated instrument-makers take rank with the most distinguished astronomers; supplying, as they do, the means by which only the latter are enabled to make these great discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and engage highly skilled instrument makers; instrument construction is as crucial to observational accuracy as theoretical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sextant suitability and operational principle for marine use
rubrics_metrics.description: The sextant is also one of the most valuable instruments for taking celestial arcs ... It is particularly valuable for measuring celestial arcs at sea, because it is not, like most astronomical instruments, affected by the motion of the ship. ... it gives the angular distance between any two bodies on the celestial sphere, by reflecting the image of one of the bodies so as to coincide with the other body, as seen directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sextants at sea for angular distances; operate by bringing reflected image to coincide with direct view, read limb via vernier/micrometer, and hold instrument firmly despite ship motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vernier and micrometer use on handheld instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The movable arm ... also carries a vernier, at D, a contrivance which, like the micrometer, enables us to take off minute parts of the spaces into which the limb is divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ verniers and micrometers on sextants and other instruments to obtain fine angular readings beyond the main limb divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand sidereal, apparent, and mean time and the equation of time
rubrics_metrics.description: The time of the earth's revolution on its axis ... is called a sidereal day. Solar time is reckoned by the apparent revolution of the sun. Mean time is time reckoned by the average length of all the solar days throughout the year. The interval by which apparent time differs from mean time, is called the equation of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct time standard for purpose: sidereal time for star-based measurements, mean solar time for civil purposes; apply the equation of time to convert apparent (solar) time to mean time when regulating clocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate astronomical clocks to sidereal time for meridian work and test frequently
rubrics_metrics.description: The astronomical clock is so regulated as to keep exact pace with the stars, and of course with the revolution of the earth on its axis; that is, it is regulated to sidereal time. ... Although astronomical clocks have been brought to a great degree of perfection, so as hardly to vary a second for many months, yet none are absolutely perfect, and most are so far from it, as to require to be corrected by means of the transit instrument, every few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate observatory clocks to sidereal time for star timing; regularly test clock uniformity and correct by transit observations (compare star passages with tables and between pairs of stars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meridian observations to assess clock uniformity and rate
rubrics_metrics.description: By taking the difference of any two stars, on successive days, it will be seen whether the going of the clock is uniform for that part of the day; and by taking the right ascensions of different pairs of stars, we may learn the rate of the clock at various parts of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform systematic meridian timing of star pairs and successive-day comparisons to detect non-uniformity or rate drift in clocks.
